posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-value ICP prospects (VP Ops, COO, CEO) engaging on a compliance-driven AI ban — validate the 'explainability' pain with a specific observation, position auditability as the real unlock
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' problem is exactly why most finance teams are quietly shelving AI tools right now — not because they don't work, but because they can't be defended in a room with a regulator. There's a difference between an answer and an auditable answer, and most AI analytics tools are only built for the first one. Curious whether the ban at your org was a permanent call or more of a 'we'll revisit when the tooling catches up' situation?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO at 140-person consultancy hitting the adoption wall with Power BI — validate the trust gap insight, add a specific observation about why finance teams default to Excel, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The trust problem is so underrated. Finance teams don't distrust the dashboard — they distrust not being able to explain where a number came from when the CFO pushes back in the room. Excel feels safer because they built it, they know every cell. Have you figured out what it would actually take for them to own the numbers the same way?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging on dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why dashboards get bloated in the first place' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: 47 KPIs is almost always a political problem dressed up as a measurement problem — every team wants their metric on the board, so nobody kills anything. The 10% to 85% jump makes complete sense to me, because people only open dashboards they actually trust to tell them something. The hard question is how you stop it creeping back to 47 the moment someone new joins the exec team.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail is engaging on a post about BI chaos — validate the 'who owns truth' pain with a sharper frame around semantic layer vs tooling, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The 200 reports problem isn't a Power BI problem, it's a 'nobody agreed on definitions before the licenses landed' problem. Giving everyone a paintbrush doesn't make everyone a painter — and it doesn't tell you which painting is right. Most teams fix this by locking things down again, which defeats the whole point. Wonder if the answer is less about who owns the tool and more about who owns the dictionary.

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO framing AI hallucinations as a security risk (not just accuracy) with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the reframe, add the trust layer insight, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and most analytics vendors are nowhere near ready for it. A wrong number in a dashboard is annoying. A hallucinated number that survives three approval layers and ends up in a board deck — that's a different category of problem entirely. I wonder how many teams even have a way to audit where an AI-generated figure actually came from.

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with BI adoption frustration — validate the £200k ghost-tool problem, add the real reason it happens, leave a sharp observation
posts.draft_comment: That £200k platform isn't broken — it's just speaking a language the business never learned. Most BI tools assume the person asking the question is the same person who modelled the data. They almost never are. The real cost isn't the licence fee, it's the year of decisions that got made on gut feel because nobody could get a straight answer out of the thing.

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a mid-market industrial firm hitting the classic 'whose numbers are right' wall — validate the cultural diagnosis, add the layer he's missing about definitions not just filters
posts.draft_comment: The filter thing is almost always a symptom. The real issue is three teams never agreed on what 'revenue this quarter' actually means in the first place — filters just make it visible. Culture fixes the behaviour, but someone still has to draw a line in the sand on definitions and own it. Who in your org is supposed to be that person?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing the 'nobody knows what to ask' problem — validate the root cause and reframe it as a data literacy issue, not a tooling issue
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number doesn't surprise me — most people don't have a clear enough mental model of their own data to know what questions are even worth asking. The shadow AI thing is interesting though. ChatGPT on a phone feels approachable because there's no stakes, no IT policy breathing down your neck. Did you find the 12% who actually used it had something in common, or was it pretty random?
